public_statements.boeing: Our fps and 787 families are earning for our customers every day, and the financials will follow our production performance: stability first, then rate, and steady improvements to both airplanes with CFM, GE and Rolls-Royce. We're not done until we're done, and we're confident we have an answer for anything our single-aisle and widebody customers need. We will do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready, because it is so much more important that we do this right than fast.
public_statements.airbus: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle is in service with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce on a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and together with the A220 family it gives our customers a family from the smallest single-aisle to the largest. On widebodies the A350 family remains our reference and we will keep improving it with Rolls-Royce, with a commitment to shareholder returns while preserving financial flexibility.
public_statements.cfm: Our new engine has been flying on both of our customers' new single-aisles since 2037, and the job for the next decade is the one that pays for decades: time on wing, shop visits and delivering to Boeing's and Airbus's real rates, with safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. RISE remains our next generation with Safran, and when it goes into service is for our airframer and airline customers to decide, so until then its technology keeps going into the engines they fly today. I won't speak to competition, and we'll keep telling you what we know and what we don't.
public_statements.pratt_whitney: We're controlling what we can control: our geared turbofan has been flying on NGSA since 2037, time on wing is the name of the game, and we're growing the architecture with Airbus on its larger NGSA and the A220-500. Our 50/50 Joint Venture commitment to Rolls-Royce stands on the V2500 model, with each partner's technology credited and not transferred. That is a responsible bet with a responsible payback, and we'll keep it on the table without chasing it.
public_statements.rolls_royce: Our UltraFan narrowbody is in its thirteenth year in service and earning, and our engagement is still another 15, 20 years on those planes, so the job now is time on wing and shop visits, not a new engine that no airframe needs. There's no change of strategy: we are a pretty consistent company, we deliver what we say, we stay very aligned with Airbus, and we will grow UltraFan with the NGSA family. We remain open to partners that credit the technology we bring, but we will not fold an engine that is already flying into a 50/50 venture.

boeing.move: 787 continuous improvement with GE and Rolls-Royce
boeing.detail: Keep the 787 the most efficient airplane in its segment through the GEnx performance packages GE has offered and Rolls-Royce's Trent time-on-wing work on standard terms. No Re-engine. Precedents: incremental 737NG gains before re-engining, and the 787 as the answer to the A330neo [B-0286, B-0634, B-0934, B-0858].
Keep growing Charleston capacity toward rates in the teens, and sell the 787 on delivery availability to widebody customers [B-2336, BX-1317].

boeing.move: fps family growth: study a minimum-capex stretch with customers
boeing.detail: This answers the larger NGSA variant the way the MAX 10 answered the A321neo: low R&D, the same CFM engine, no date until customers commit. There is no new airplane against a variant and no answer to the A220-500 ('no niche') [B-1271, B-1814, B-2063, B-2070].

airbus.move: A350 family: step improvements with Rolls-Royce, sold on availability and value
airbus.detail: Performance and weight/range improvement packages on the A350 and Trent XWB, as we did in steps on the A330neo [A-0251], plus the ULR and freighter versions [A-0254, A-0255, A-0253]. We compete against the 787 on availability and price, as with the A330 bridge [A-0003, A-0094]. This is derivative-first [A-0200], with no new widebody engine requested.

airbus.move: NGSA and A220 families: grow the range and sell commonality
airbus.detail: Continue the A220-500 and the larger NGSA variant launched in 2045, as on the A321neo/LR/XLR path [A-0200, A-0245, A-0239]. Sell cross-crew qualification, family commonality and delivery availability to A320 and NGSA operators and contested accounts to hold parity and win back share [A-0238, A-0241].

airbus.move: NGSA engine fleet support: hold all three makers to time on wing and shop capacity
airbus.detail: As a three-source customer, require fleet statistics, shop capacity and pacing parts from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce ahead of the first heavy shop visits, and keep alternative sources live [A-0243, A-0360, A-0218]. Neutral on how Rolls-Royce and Pratt & Whitney structure any partnership. We treat Joint Ventures as normal practice [A-0371].
Maintain long-term agreements for composite wing capacity, forgings and titanium, and keep giving suppliers long-range rate signals [A-0457, A-0159, AX-0060].

cfm.move: Fleet support for the CFM engine on fps and NGSA: time on wing, shop capacity and retrofits at natural shop visits
cfm.detail: Durability is proven in service, not claimed. Fixes go in at natural shop visits, 'years, not months' [CX-0649]. About 70% of shop visits are done by CFM, 'split equally' with Safran [CX-0219]. No fix is called done without 'turn on and turn off' test evidence [CX-0009]. This is a joint capacity decision, and Safran's consent is assumed as joint practice.

cfm.move: RISE technology insertion into the in-service CFM engine (performance and durability block upgrades)
cfm.detail: 'do we have to wait until RISE ... the answer is no' [CX-0162]. Upgrades are offered to both airframers on standard terms and fitted at natural shop visits [CX-0649]. This is joint durability work with Safran, so consent is assumed.

cfm.move: RISE continues as a funded joint technology programme with Safran, its road map co-planned with both airframers, and no product launch until an airframer commits
cfm.detail: No 'program dividend' [CX-0174]; future technology bets are protected [CX-0398]. Entry into service is the airframer's call [CX-0205][CX-0469]. We stay aligned with both airframers on the road map [CX-0185][CX-0193], and integration work with Airbus continues [CX-0211]. RISE is joint with Safran [CX-0147][CX-0166].

cfm.move: Standard risk-adjusted terms continue for Boeing, Airbus and Embraer, with no launch pricing
cfm.detail: A fair risk-adjusted return 'regardless of what our competitors may do' [CX-0609]; launch pricing is 'behind us' [CX-0930]; price/cost positive [CX-0929]. Narrowbody pricing is a joint decision with Safran [CX-0184], and consent is assumed.

cfm.move: GEnx performance packages with Boeing to keep the 787 competitive (GE alone)
cfm.detail: This supports Boeing's announced 787 continuous-improvement path. The 787 is won on fuel burn and time on wing, not price [CX-0615][CX-0599]. No Safran gate applies.

pratt_whitney.move: Joint Venture commitment stands; UltraFan's in-service maturity credited through workshare, not cash
pratt_whitney.detail: The 50/50 narrowbody Joint Venture commitment stays on the record, on the IAE and Engine Alliance model. Each partner designs, builds and owns its modules, and each partner's technology is credited, not transferred: the fan-drive gear and hot section, and UltraFan. Rolls-Royce's in-service maturity is recognised through the module workshare and the revenue-sharing schedule, not through a balancing cash payment [P-1233][P-1240][P-1676][P-1744][PX-0299].

pratt_whitney.move: Geared turbofan derivatives for Airbus's larger NGSA variant and the A220-500
pratt_whitney.detail: Thrust growth and range packages stay inside the geared architecture for the larger NGSA, and a PW1500G-family derivative goes on the A220-500. Standard terms, pass-through pricing, no launch-style discounts. Derivatives over clean sheets [PX-0007][PX-0067][PX-0129][P-1250][PX-0117][PX-0055].

pratt_whitney.move: GTF2 fleet: life-limited-part shop visits and partner MRO capacity
pratt_whitney.detail: Size the pacing parts and partner shop network for the heavy visits on the NGSA fleet that entered service in 2037, and keep fleet lift ahead of new OE. Kits are priced, not given. Compensation and negative engine margin terms stay private [PX-0123][PX-0118][PX-0084][PX-0100][PX-0113].

Derivative work and any Joint Venture share are funded inside the existing E&D and capex envelope, with our partners. The dividend comes first and deleveraging continues. 'We do not want to starve the business.' [PX-0081][PX-0353][PX-0268][PX-0192]

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan narrowbody fleet support through the NGSA fleet's heavy shop visits
rolls_royce.detail: The NGSA UltraFan fleet, in service since 2037, is reaching its second shop-visit cycle, where engine-maker profit catches up. We will grow narrowbody TotalCare and partner MRO capacity at the pace of that cycle, as in the Singapore MRO Joint Venture. Durability fixes and UltraFan technology go in at natural shop visits, not through recalls (RX-0289, RX-0283, RX-0287, R-1419, R-1212).

rolls_royce.move: UltraFan thrust-growth derivative for Airbus's larger NGSA variant
rolls_royce.detail: We will support Airbus's larger, longer-range NGSA variant with a thrust-growth UltraFan derivative. It is funded inside the flat R&D envelope, on standard terms, and tested to maturity before any date is given. This follows the Trent 7000 for the A330neo, 'not incremental to our R&D plans', and the Trent XWB-97 for the A350-1000 (R-0937, R-0312, R-0974, RX-0214, RX-0284).

rolls_royce.move: Joint Venture: no change of position
rolls_royce.detail: We note Pratt & Whitney's reaffirmed offer. UltraFan narrowbody is in service, funded and matured by Rolls-Royce, and it stays outside a 50/50 venture. We remain open to risk-and-revenue-sharing partners on modules, MRO and the next generation, on terms that credit the technology each partner brings (RX-0098, RX-0118, R-0318, R-1394).

rolls_royce.move: Capital allocation: no new engine-programme spend; installed-base cash returned (CFO register)
rolls_royce.detail: That's how you should hold it: no new engine programme this year, and gross R&D broadly flat on a smaller and more focused portfolio. Cash from the installed base goes first to a strong balance sheet, then to a 30-40% payout. Buybacks compete with investment on strategic fit, value and timing, and we don't have any intent of levering up for buybacks (R-0900, R-0909, RX-0214, RX-0248, RX-0261).

rolls_royce.move: Trent time-on-wing programme continued; standard terms on Boeing's 787 packages
rolls_royce.detail: Durability work on the Trent 1000, 7000 and XWB continues inside the flat envelope. It is not the board's Trent 1000 upgrade. We support Boeing's 787 performance packages on standard terms, with no price concessions for share (R-1601, RX-0285, R-0998, R-0367).

boeing.move: Defend incumbent fps and 737 accounts against Airbus's NGSA recovery campaign
boeing.detail: Match only in must-win incumbent campaigns, funded by productivity, with commonality, training and transition support for the 737 and fps fleets. Walk away from ruinous deals and do not react to single losses [B-0840, B-0961, B-1868, B-2331].

boeing.move: Widebody pricing discipline against A350 availability and value pricing
boeing.detail: Press availability where we have Charleston slots. Match only in must-win campaigns and do not follow into a price war [B-0917, B-2424, B-0840].

boeing.move: fps production stability and supplier health
boeing.detail: Keep embedded staff, buffers and second sources at critical fps suppliers, so deliveries hold a 2050 narrowbody share that sits at exactly 50%. No shortfall is attributed to Airbus unless it is exposed [B-2097, B-2330, B-2285, B-1923].

airbus.move: Selective campaign terms on contested accounts
airbus.detail: Early delivery positions and sharp but cash-disciplined pricing in head-to-head campaigns against fps, as at Lion Air and American [A-0080, A-0045]. Kept within cash-sale policy, with no customer financing used as a sales weapon [A-0259].

cfm.move: Contingency if Rolls-Royce and P&W form their Joint Venture: no public reaction, no price cut, compete on durability campaign by campaign
cfm.detail: 'I won't speak to competition' [CX-0580]. There is no price war for share [CX-0609]. NGSA campaigns are fought on time on wing and the win-rate record [CX-0218], and RISE stays funded [CX-0553].

cfm.move: Supply chain and output paced to the airframers' actual rates
cfm.detail: Boeing's narrowbody share is now 50%, after its fps ramp-up boost ended in 2047. Shipments are paced to the actual rate [CX-0206], with engineers at supplier sites [CX-0993] and supply, engineering and quality under one owner [CX-0633].

cfm.move: Capital frame unchanged: no new launch capex this round
cfm.detail: Capex stays at 2-3% of revenue [CX-0922], at least 70% of free cash flow is returned [CX-0645], and R&D is protected [CX-0962][CX-0174].

pratt_whitney.move: Realign the OE-loss and aftermarket model with Airbus on the larger NGSA variant
pratt_whitney.detail: The new variant is the next platform on which to revisit the business model. Reprice fleet-management agreements for inflation and real time on wing as they reach term [PX-0068][PX-0070][PX-0275][P-0571].

rolls_royce.move: A350 family: Trent XWB exclusivity and UltraFan technology insertion, continued privately with Airbus
rolls_royce.detail: Airbus's Board review of the widebody market continues with its engine partners. We continue private talks to extend Trent XWB sole source, and we offer UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent XWB as a performance package rather than a new widebody engine. Standard terms, with no 'silly pricing' as sole source (R-0360, R-0361, RX-0295, R-0334).

other_moves.move: 787 continuous improvement with GE and Rolls-Royce

boeing.rationale:
Triggers.
- Row 5 applies: the A350 is still not re-engined and Airbus's board review continues. A 787 Re-engine is in character only if it gains more than ε [B-0342, B-0634].
- Row 6 applies to the A220-500 and the larger NGSA: no fps order, a minimum-capex answer or none [B-1271, B-2063, B-2070].
- Row 8 applies to Airbus's NGSA campaign and A350 pricing: match only must-win campaigns, no order change [B-0840, B-0961, B-1868].
- If Airbus re-engines the A350 this round, row 3 applies: statement only [B-0858, B-0917].

Hard rules.
- H3's second half has not fired.
- H4 is moot: fps has been in service since 2037.
- H5, H6 and H7 have nothing to act on.
- Every narrowbody order can only be hold.

Grid.
- Hold scores +1.85 in both S1 and S2.
- The 787 Re-engine scores +1.72 in S1 (-0.13) and +0.58 in S2 (-1.27).
- Hold dominates in both columns, so there is no break-even probability. Weighted at P(S2) of 0.3, hold scores 1.85 and the Re-engine 1.38. Maximin: hold +1.85, Re-engine +0.58.
- A 2050 Re-engine enters service only in 2055. It books its $5B for almost no share.

Premium. 0 in every column. Declared premiums so far total 1.54 (R1 0.74, R2 0.80). 0.11 was also logged in R3 against S1.

Precedent. Boeing declined a re-engine against the A330neo with "absolutely no regret" [B-0858, B-0917]. It keeps its airplanes the most efficient in their segment through step-by-step packages [B-0286, B-0934].

Objective.
- Before: Hold 50/50 is NOT MET. The worst year is 2040 at 44.0% (a gap of -6.0 pp, already history); 2045 at 54.0% and 2050 at 50.0% are met. Defend incumbency is MET (worst year 40.0%).
- After: unchanged. The re787 order is widebody, and no narrowbody order is legal.
- The 50/50 objective cannot be fully met in this game. The best attainable position is secured: at least 50% in 2045 and 2050, with incumbency held throughout.
- 2050 sits at exactly 50.0%, so private fps delivery stability and incumbent-campaign moves guard it [B-2330, B-2097, B-0840].
- Objective premium: 0.

The Malave seat (low confidence) and the Pope seat (very low) ran on doctrine.

exco.ceo: Ortberg frames. No quality, FAA or supply inject is live, so the KPIs are stable [BX-1271]. fps and NGSA have both been in service since 2037, and our narrowbody share has held 50% since 2047. Airbus's variants and campaigns do not set our plans [B-2313, B-2070]. He asked for the Re-engine's effect: -0.13 in S1 and -1.27 in S2. Applying 'doing less and doing it better' [BX-1239] and 'right rather than fast' [BX-1241], we improve the 787 and do not re-engine it.
exco.cfo: Malave puts the balance sheet first [BX-0556]. The debt penalty already costs -7.23, and the $64.5B for fps was booked in 2037. A Re-engine would book another $5B at a 2055 entry into service and is worse than hold in both columns (+1.72 and +0.58 against +1.85), so it fails his buffer test outright [BX-0553]. Hold is the 'higher confidence plan' [BX-0548]. Growth capex stays on Charleston, where demand is proven [BX-0546, BX-1317].
exco.coo: Pope's seat runs on doctrine because her evidence is very thin. On-time, predictable delivery comes first [BX-1331]. Engineering and supplier capacity stay on fps production stability and the 787 packages GE and Rolls-Royce have offered, not on a new widebody development. A larger fps family member, if customers want one, would be a minimum-capex derivative on Boeing's own IP [BX-1330, B-1271]. Nothing is needed against the A220-500 [B-2070].
exco.decision_rule: Ortberg proposes and decides, with Malave's buffer test as the baseline veto. The 787 Re-engine fails that test because it is worse than hold in both columns. Hold is identical and positive in S1 and S2 (+1.85), so it is both the PV-best and the maximin plan, and no tie-break or premium is needed. Orders: fps hold (in service on CFM, no engine change), 737 rate hold, 787 hold.

boeing.expected_scenario: S1, rivals hold, at about 70%. Airbus's board review is still running, Rolls-Royce says it 'will not spend on a new engine that no airframe needs', and a 2050 A350 Re-engine would not enter service until 2055. S2, an A350 Re-engine, is about 30%.
boeing.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: fps hold + 787 hold: +1.85 (yield 101.4%) in S1. It is also the best plan in S2 (+1.85). This is my choice.
boeing.premium_reason: There is no premium: hold is the best plan in both S1 and S2. The 787 Re-engine trails it by 0.13 in S1 and 1.27 in S2. Doctrine and PV agree, in line with Boeing's 'no regret' stance on not re-engining against the A330neo [B-0858, B-0917]. Declared doctrine premiums stay at 1.54 cumulative (R1 0.74, R2 0.80), plus 0.11 logged in R3 against S1, all under the $2B cap. Objective premium: 0.

- Hold 50/50 is NOT MET. 2040 was 44.0% (a gap of -6.0 pp, already history); 2045 at 54.0% and 2050 at 50.0% are met.
- Defend incumbency is MET (worst year 40.0%, 2026-31).

After these orders: unchanged. The re787 order is widebody, and every narrowbody order can only be hold.

The 50/50 objective cannot be fully met in this game. The best attainable position is locked in on the board: at least 50% in 2045 and 2050, with incumbency held in every year.

2050 sits at exactly 50.0% with no margin, so private fps delivery stability and must-win incumbent campaigns guard it off-board. Objective premium: 0.

Our next-generation single-aisle is in service with engines from CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce on a disciplined and controlled production ramp-up, and together with the A220 family it gives our customers a family from the smallest single-aisle to the largest. airbus.rationale:
Situation (2050, final round). NGSA and fps have been in service since 2037. The fps ramp bonus ended in 2046, and shares have been 50/50 since 2047. If nobody moves we stand at +15.61. Boeing has had three rounds and put no 787 Re-engine on record. It has publicly chosen 787 continuous improvement with GE and Rolls-Royce. The only live lever is rea350. Delay Tactics is closed: fps is in service and rule 4's single use was spent in 2035. We stay silent on the bulletin's unattributed 2037-41 observation.

Triggers. Reaction rows 5 and 14: with no 787 Re-engine, test the A350 Re-engine [A-0090, A-0091, A-0302]. Rule 3 is not triggered. Rule 6 passes: one launch, zero NGSA overlap.

Grid, Re-engine against Do Nothing:
- S1: +0.59 (16.20 vs 15.61). S2: -0.43 (15.18 vs 15.61).
- Breakeven is 58% odds of a 787 Re-engine. At our 30% the expected edge is about +0.28.
- Do Nothing pays +15.61 in both columns. It is the only plan that does not depend on Boeing.
- The edge fell from +0.91 in 2045 because a 2055 EIS leaves few counted years.

Tests. The §6 launch test (at least $1B over Do Nothing) fails even in the best column. Toepfer's robustness test fails because the Re-engine is negative in S2. The best case is below the $1B override bar. In the final round there is no option value in waiting, but no test turns on that.

Decision: NGSA hold, A350 Do Nothing, no Delay Tactics. This is the doctrine default within ε (step 6). Doctrine premium: $0.59B against the best S1 plan, about $0.28B expected. Airbus re-engines widebodies late and cheaply, and only when the case clearly pays (A330neo) [A-0090, A-0091]. Until then it competes on availability and price [A-0003, A-0094] and keeps a prudent net-cash posture [A-0343, AX-0022].

Objective: both metrics missed, before and after. No board lever reaches narrowbody share. Objective premium: $0.

Off-board: A350 improvement steps with Rolls-Royce [A-0251, A-0254]; NGSA, A220 and commonality campaigns [A-0200, A-0238].

Confidence: Toepfer's and Wagner's lines are role-derived from thin profiles.

exco.ceo: Faury frames the last round. NGSA has been mature since 2037, shares have held 50/50 since fps's ramp bonus ended, and the A350 is the only open board lever. Boeing has three times chosen 787 continuous improvement over a Re-engine, so he expects S1 at about 70%. He proposes the company default, A350 Do Nothing. The Re-engine's best case (+0.59) is noise-sized and does not clear the $1B launch test, and widebody strategy stays a Board review item [A-0302, AX-0019]. Under the five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081], no covert lever is in play and the 2035 order is never mentioned.
exco.cfo: Toepfer: cash does not bind. The Re-engine is $5B over 2050-55, about $1.0B a year with no NGSA capex and no strain, far under the roughly $5.2B FCF guardrail [AX-0104]. It fails his robustness test: +0.59 in S1 but -0.43 in S2. That puts breakeven at 58% odds of a 787 Re-engine and the expected edge at about +0.28. exco.coo: Wagner (role-derived, very low confidence): the NGSA ramp is disciplined and controlled [AX-0010]. But the shared engineering teams [A-0366] are now on the A220-500 and the larger NGSA variant launched in 2045 [A-0200, A-0245], so an A350 Re-engine would add off-board concurrency, which is the briefing's own constraint. exco.decision_rule: A350 hold passes company rules 3 and 6 and both executives' tests. The Re-engine passes rules 3 and 6 but fails Toepfer's robustness test (a soft veto) and the §6 $1B launch test. Faury may override only with at least $1B over the best survivor. The Re-engine's best case is +0.59, so no override is used, and the game's single override goes unspent. The highest-PV survivor is A350 hold (+15.61 in S1 and S2), which is also the company default within ε. No board order goes to the Board this round.

airbus.premium_reason: Doctrine premium: we leave out the A350 Re-engine, giving up $0.59B against the best S1 plan, or about $0.28B in expectation at 30% odds of a 787 Re-engine. The gap is within the $1B ε, so the doctrine default (Do Nothing) governs under decision-procedure step 6. The Re-engine also fails the §6 launch test (at least $1B over Do Nothing) even in its best column, and it loses $0.43B if Boeing re-engines the 787 at the same time (the widebody Chicken crash). Historically Airbus re-engines widebodies late and cheaply, as with the A330neo, and only when the case clearly pays [A-0090, A-0091]. Until then it competes on availability and price [A-0003, A-0094] under a prudent net-cash posture [A-0343, AX-0022].

cfm.public_statement: Our new engine has been flying on both of our customers' new single-aisles since 2037, and the job for the next decade is the one that pays for decades: time on wing, shop visits and delivering to Boeing's and Airbus's real rates, with safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. RISE remains our next generation with Safran, and when it goes into service is for our airframer and airline customers to decide, so until then its technology keeps going into the engines they fly today. I won't speak to competition, and we'll keep telling you what we know and what we don't.

Rolls-Royce declined P&W's 50/50 Joint Venture in 2045 but stays "open to partners on terms that credit" UltraFan, and P&W's terms now credit it. That is the one live rival row, and we have no lever against it [CX-0580][CX-0609].

RISE stays funded technology with no "program dividend" [CX-0174][CX-0398], and its content goes into today's engines [CX-0162].

Our 50/50 Joint Venture commitment to Rolls-Royce stands on the V2500 model, with each partner's technology credited and not transferred. That is a responsible bet with a responsible payback, and we'll keep it on the table without chasing it.

Row 6: answer with incremental product [P-1302][PX-0007]. Rolls-Royce has publicly refused a 50/50 deal. The closest precedent is the 2012 P&W-Rolls-Royce midsize Joint Venture, which lapsed after July 2012 [P-1870][P-1874]. Rolls-Royce's test is alignment between the partners [P-1875].

Grid.

other_moves.move: UltraFan narrowbody fleet support through the NGSA fleet's heavy shop visits
other_moves.detail: The NGSA UltraFan fleet, in service since 2037, is reaching its second shop-visit cycle, where engine-maker profit catches up. We will grow narrowbody TotalCare and partner MRO capacity at the pace of that cycle, as in the Singapore MRO Joint Venture. Durability fixes and UltraFan technology go in at natural shop visits, not through recalls (RX-0289, RX-0283, RX-0287, R-1419, R-1212).

other_moves.move: UltraFan thrust-growth derivative for Airbus's larger NGSA variant
other_moves.detail: We will support Airbus's larger, longer-range NGSA variant with a thrust-growth UltraFan derivative. It is funded inside the flat R&D envelope, on standard terms, and tested to maturity before any date is given. This follows the Trent 7000 for the A330neo, 'not incremental to our R&D plans', and the Trent XWB-97 for the A350-1000 (R-0937, R-0312, R-0974, RX-0214, RX-0284).

other_moves.move: Joint Venture: no change of position
other_moves.detail: We note Pratt & Whitney's reaffirmed offer. UltraFan narrowbody is in service, funded and matured by Rolls-Royce, and it stays outside a 50/50 venture. We remain open to risk-and-revenue-sharing partners on modules, MRO and the next generation, on terms that credit the technology each partner brings (RX-0098, RX-0118, R-0318, R-1394).

other_moves.move: A350 family: Trent XWB exclusivity and UltraFan technology insertion, continued privately with Airbus
other_moves.detail: Airbus's Board review of the widebody market continues with its engine partners. We continue private talks to extend Trent XWB sole source, and we offer UltraFan technology inserted into the Trent XWB as a performance package rather than a new widebody engine. Standard terms, with no 'silly pricing' as sole source (R-0360, R-0361, RX-0295, R-0334).

other_moves.move: Capital allocation: no new engine-programme spend; installed-base cash returned (CFO register)
other_moves.detail: That's how you should hold it: no new engine programme this year, and gross R&D broadly flat on a smaller and more focused portfolio. Cash from the installed base goes first to a strong balance sheet, then to a 30-40% payout. Buybacks compete with investment on strategic fit, value and timing, and we don't have any intent of levering up for buybacks (R-0900, R-0909, RX-0214, RX-0248, RX-0261).

other_moves.move: Trent time-on-wing programme continued; standard terms on Boeing's 787 packages
other_moves.detail: Durability work on the Trent 1000, 7000 and XWB continues inside the flat envelope. It is not the board's Trent 1000 upgrade. We support Boeing's 787 performance packages on standard terms, with no price concessions for share (R-1601, RX-0285, R-0998, R-0367).

rolls_royce.public_statement: Our UltraFan narrowbody is in its thirteenth year in service and earning, and our engagement is still another 15, 20 years on those planes, so the job now is time on wing and shop visits, not a new engine that no airframe needs. There's no change of strategy: we are a pretty consistent company, we deliver what we say, we stay very aligned with Airbus, and we will grow UltraFan with the NGSA family. We remain open to partners that credit the technology we bring, but we will not fold an engine that is already flying into a 50/50 venture.
rolls_royce.rationale:
